en: The Analysis of the Vibhaṅga: The Analysis of the Right Strivings (Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga) 1.
The Exposition according to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya)
The four right efforts:

here, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; [and for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states...]
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of unwholesome states;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states;
and for the stability, non-confusion, and further increase of arisen wholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for their increase, development, and fulfillment.
And how does a bhikkhu generate desire, exert himself, arouse energy, apply his mind, and strive for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states?
In this regard, what are the unarisen evil, unwholesome states?
The three unwholesome roots:
greed, hatred, and delusion,
as well as the defilements associated with them.
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with that [craving],
as well as the bodily, verbal, and mental actions originating from it—
these are called "unarisen evil unwholesome states."
Thus, for the sake of the non-arising of these unarisen evil, unwholesome states, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives.
“He generates desire”:
therein, what is desire?
Whatever desire, state of desiring, wish to act, and wholesome desire for the Dhamma there is—
this is called "desire. One generates this desire,
produces it, arouses it, fully arouses it, brings it about, and fully brings it about.
Therefore it is said: “He generates desire.
“He exerts effort.
In this context, what is effort?
That which is the mental arousal of energy …pe… right effort—
this is called "effort.
By means of this effort, he is endowed with it, fully endowed with it, approached it, fully approached it, attained it, perfected it, and possessed of it.
Therefore it is said:
“He exerts himself,” and “He arouses energy.
In this context, what is energy?
That which is the mental arousal of energy … [as above] … right effort—
this is called "energy.
One arouses this energy, fully arouses it, pursues it, develops it, and cultivates it frequently.
Therefore it is said: "He arouses energy" and "he uplifts the mind.
In this context, what is the mind?
That which is mind, mentation, the mental faculty …pe… the corresponding element of mind-consciousness—
this is called "mind.
One uplifts this mind, fully uplifts it, supports it, and firmly supports it.
Therefore it is said, “he exerts the mind.
[It is said,] “he strives.
In this context, what is striving?
That which is the mental arousal of energy …pe… right effort—
this is called "exertion.
By means of this exertion, he is endowed with it …pe… possessed of it.
Therefore it is said, “he strives.
And how does a bhikkhu generate desire, exert himself, arouse energy, apply his mind, and strive for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen?
In this context, what are the evil, unwholesome states that have arisen?
The three unwholesome roots:
greed, hatred, and delusion,
as well as the defilements associated with them.

The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with that [craving], as well as the bodily, verbal, and mental actions originated by it—
these are called "arisen evil unwholesome states. Thus,
for the sake of abandoning these arisen evil unwholesome states, one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, uplifts the mind, and strives.
“He generates desire.
In this context, what is desire?
It is that which is desire, the state of desiring, the wish to act, wholesome desire for the Dhamma.
This is called "desire.
One generates this desire, fully generates it, arouses it, fully arouses it, produces it, and brings it forth.
Therefore, it is said: "one generates desire."
“Exertion. In this context, what is exertion?
It is the arousal of mental energy … [as before] … right effort.
This is called "effort.
One is possessed of this effort ... [as before] ... endowed with it.
Therefore, one is said to "exert effort."
“He arouses energy.
In this context, what is energy?
It is that which is the arousal of mental energy … [and so on] … right effort.
This is called "energy.
One initiates this energy, undertakes it, pursues it, develops it, and cultivates it frequently.
Therefore, it is said: "one initiates energy."
“He exerts the mind.
In this context, what is the mind?
That which is mind, mentality, mentation … [as above] … the corresponding element of mind-consciousness.
This is called "the mind.
One uplifts this mind, fully uplifts it, supports it, and firmly supports it.
Therefore, it is said, "one uplifts the mind."
“Exertion. In this context, what is exertion?
It is the arousal of mental energy … [as above] … right effort.
This is called "exertion.
By means of this exertion, he is endowed with it... possessed of it.
Therefore, he is said to "exert himself."
And how does a bhikkhu generate desire, exert effort, arouse energy, apply his mind, and strive for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen?
In this context, what are the wholesome states that have not yet arisen?
They are the three roots of wholesomeness.
Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;

the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with them; and the bodily, verbal, and mental actions originating from them—these are called "wholesome states that have not yet arisen."
Thus, for the arising of these unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives.
“He generates desire” ... [as before] ...
“he exerts himself” ... [as before].
“He arouses energy,” ...
“he exerts the mind,” ...
“he strives.”
In this context, what is striving?
That which is the arousal of mental energy …pe… right effort—
this is called “striving.”
By means of this striving he is endowed with it... possessed of it.
Therefore he is said to "strive.

And how does a bhikkhu generate desire, exert himself, arouse energy, apply his mind, and strive for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen?
In this context, what are the arisen wholesome states?
They are the three wholesome roots:
non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with that [mind], as well as the bodily, verbal, and mental actions originating from it— these are called "arisen wholesome states.

Thus, for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of these arisen wholesome states, one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, uplifts the mind, and strives.

“For stability”: that which is stability is non-confusion; that which is non-confusion is increase; that which is increase is abundance; that which is abundance is development; that which is development is fulfillment.
“He generates desire,” and so forth.
“He exerts effort,” …pe… “he arouses energy,” …pe… “he uplifts the mind,” …pe…
"It exerts" (padahati).
In that regard, what is exertion (padhāna)?
It is the arousal of mental energy, ... [as above] ... right effort.
This is called "exertion.
By means of this exertion, he is endowed with it... [as before] ...possessed of it.
Therefore, he is said to "exert himself."
The Exposition of the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya). 2.
The Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya):
The four right endeavors (cattāro sammappadhānā)—

Here, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;

he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.
And how does a bhikkhu generate desire, exert himself, arouse energy, apply his mind, and strive for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the destruction [of the taints], and results in the attainment of the first stage, for the abandoning of views—being quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [he] enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna.

He dwells in a practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; at that time, for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives.
"He generates desire" means:
In this context, what is zeal (*chanda*)?
That which is zeal, the state of being zealous, the desire to act, and wholesome zeal for the Dhamma—
this is called “zeal.”
He generates this desire, produces it, arouses it, fully arouses it, brings it forth, and brings it to manifestation.
Therefore it is said: "he generates desire.
"He exerts effort": [this refers to that].
Therein, what is effort?
That which is the arousal of mental energy …pe… right effort, the enlightenment factor of energy, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "effort."
By means of this effort, he is endowed, fully endowed, approached, fully approached, attained, perfected, and possessed of it.
Therefore, it is said:
"He exerts himself" and "he arouses energy."
In this context, what is energy?
That which is the arousal of mental energy … [as above] … right effort, the energy factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "energy."
One arouses this energy, exerts it, pursues it, develops it, and cultivates it extensively.
Therefore, it is said: "One arouses energy.
"One uplifts the mind."
Therein, what is consciousness?
That which is consciousness, mind, mentation …pe… the corresponding element of mind-consciousness—
this is called "consciousness."
He uplifts this mind, fully uplifts it, supports it, and firmly supports it.
Therefore it is said: "he uplifts the mind.
"He exerts himself" means:
Therein, what is right effort?
That which is the arousal of mental energy … [as above] … right exertion, the enlightenment factor of energy, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "right effort."
The remaining factors are associated with the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).
And how does a bhikkhu generate desire, exert himself, arouse energy, apply his mind, and strive for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction of the acquisitions (*apacayagāmi*), [free] from views...
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures...
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge;
at that time, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen.
“He generates desire,” ...
“he exerts effort,” ...
“he arouses energy,” ... [and so on].
“He exerts the mind” ... pe ...
“he strives.
In this context, what is right striving?
That which is the mental application of energy … [as above] … right effort, the factor of enlightenment of energy, a factor of the path included within the path—
this is called "right exertion.
All remaining phenomena are associated with right exertion.
And how does a bhikkhu generate desire, exert effort, arouse energy, apply his mind, and strive for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna—leading to liberation, leading to the waning of existence—for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so on] ...having attained the first jhāna.

He dwells in a practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; at that time, for the arising of wholesome states not yet arisen, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives.

“Striving. In this context, what is right striving?
It is the arousal of mental energy … [as before] … right effort, the enlightenment factor of energy, a factor of the path, included within the path.
This is called "right exertion" (*sammappadhāna*).
All remaining phenomena are associated with right exertion.

And how does a bhikkhu generate desire, exert himself, arouse energy, apply his mind, and strive for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen?
Here, bhikkhu, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the destruction [of the taints],
for the abandoning of views, for the attainment of the first stage— being quite secluded from sensual pleasures … he enters and dwells in the first jhāna,
which is difficult progress and slow knowledge— at that time, regarding the wholesome states that have arisen:

“For the sake of stability, for non-confusion, for increase, for abundance, for development, and for fulfillment, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. Thus it is said:
“For the sake of stability.”

That which is stability is non-confusion; that which is non-confusion is increase; that which is increase is expansion; that which is expansion is development; that which is development is fulfillment.
“He generates desire. In this context, what is desire?
Whatever desire, state of desiring, wish to act, and wholesome desire for the Dhamma there is—
this is called "desire. One generates this desire,
brings it forth, rouses it, fully rouses it, produces it, and brings it to manifestation.
Therefore it is said: “He generates desire.
“He exerts effort”:
therein, what is effort?
That which is the mental arousal of energy … right effort, the factor of enlightenment of energy, a factor of the path included within the path—
this is called "effort.
One is endowed with this effort … possessed of it.
Therefore it is said:
"He exerts himself" and "he arouses energy.
In this context, what is energy?
That which is the arousal of mental energy … right effort, the factor of enlightenment of energy, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "energy.
One arouses this energy, fully arouses it, pursues it, develops it, and cultivates it frequently.
Therefore it is said, “he arouses energy” and “he exerts the mind.
In this context, what is the mind?
That which is mind, intellect, mentation … [as above] … the corresponding mind-consciousness element—
this is called "mind.
One uplifts this mind, fully uplifts it, supports it, and firmly supports it.
Therefore it is said: "He exerts the mind. [It is said:
"He strives.
In this context, what is right effort (sammappadhāna)?
That which is the mental arousal of energy … [as above] … right effort, the energy factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "right exertion.
All remaining phenomena are associated with right exertion.
In this context, what is right effort?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the destruction [of the defilements], and is for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage—secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so forth]... having attained the first jhāna.
He dwells in a practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; at that time, whatever mental arousal of energy there is—[and so on]...
right effort, the energy factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path—this is called "right exertion."
The remaining states are associated with the right efforts.
The Exposition of the Abhidhamma. 3.
The Interrogation by Questions.
The four right strivings:

here, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; [and he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives] for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states...

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of unwholesome states; ... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; ... and for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states.
Of the four right efforts, how many are wholesome, how many unwholesome, and how many indeterminate …pe… how many are with conflict (*saraṇa*), and how many are without conflict (*araṇa*)? 3.1.
The Triplet:
They are exclusively wholesome.
They may be associated with pleasant feeling; they may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
They are of the nature to ripen as kamma-results.
They are not acquired through clinging, nor are they objects of clinging.
They are undefiled and non-defiling.

They may be accompanied by both initial application and sustained application, or they may be without initial application and have only sustained application, or they may be without both initial application and sustained application.
They may be accompanied by rapture, or they may be accompanied by pleasure, or they may be accompanied by equanimity.
Not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
Not having roots to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
Leading to the diminution [of existence].
They are for those in training; they are immeasurable;
they have immeasurable objects.
Exalted.
Fixed in rightness.
Not having the Path as its object, but having the Path as its cause; it may have the Path as its predominance, or it may not be said to have the Path as its predominance.
They may have arisen, they may not have arisen, and they should not be called "subject to arising.
They may be past, they may be future, or they may be present.
They should not be called "having a past object," nor "having a future object," nor "having a present object."
They may be internal, they may be external, or they may be both internal and external.
They have external objects.
They are non-manifest and non-reacting.
Hetugocchaka: Not roots.
They have a cause.
They are associated with a cause.
They should not be said to be both causes and having-a-cause; rather, they are having-a-cause but are not causes.
They should not be described as both roots and associated with roots; rather, they are associated with roots but are not roots themselves.
They are not roots, yet they are accompanied by roots.
3.2.2. The Minor Intermediate Dyads.
With conditions.
Conditioned.
Non-manifesting.
Non-reactive.
Formless.
Supramundane.
To be cognized by some; not to be cognized by others.
3.2.3. The Group on Taints (Āsava):
Not taints.
They are without taints (*anāsava*). They are dissociated from the taints (*āsava-vippayutta*).
They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not taints."
They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not taints.
They are dissociated from taints; they are without taints.
8.3.2.4. The Group on Fetters, etc.
There are no fetters … pe … there are no ties … pe …
...no floods ...pe...
no yokes ...pe...
no hindrances ...pe...
They are not misapprehensions ... [and so on] ...
they have an object.
They are not consciousness.
Mental factors.
Associated with consciousness.
Conjoined with consciousness.
Arising from consciousness;
co-existent with consciousness;
following after consciousness.
Conjoined with and originated by the mind;
co-existent with that which is conjoined with and originated by the mind;
accompanying that which is conjoined with and originated by the mind.
External.
Not derived from clinging. Not clung to.
8.3.2.11. The Group on Grasping (Upādāna-gocchaka), etc.:
They are not graspings … [and so on] … they are not defilements … [and so on] …
They are not to be abandoned by vision.
They are not to be abandoned by cultivation.
They do not have roots that are to be abandoned by vision.
They have roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
They may be with applied thought, or they may be without applied thought.
They may be with sustained thought, or they may be without sustained thought.
It may be with zest, or it may be without zest.
It may be accompanied by rapture, or it may not be accompanied by rapture.
It may be accompanied by pleasure, or it may not be accompanied by pleasure.
It may be accompanied by equanimity; it may not be accompanied by equanimity.
It is not of the sense sphere;
it is not of the fine-material sphere.
They do not belong to the formless realm;
they are not included within the mundane; they are conducive to liberation.
It is fixed.
It is unsurpassed.
It is without conflict.
The Section on Questioning.
The Analysis of the Right Strivings is finished.
